papers.title: Validation-guided active learning for scientific machine learning under hidden distribution shift
papers.abstract: Abstract Active learning under hidden distribution shift requires selecting samples without access to the deployment distribution. We formalize this setting and introduce Composite Active Data Acquisition for Out-of-Distribution Generalization (CADA-OOD). Its central mechanism, validation error relevance, links unlabeled candidates to current model failures on an accessible validation set. Additional terms capture predictive uncertainty and group novelty while controlling batch redundancy and outlier selection. We report a retrospective evaluation on seven molecular and materials property prediction benchmarks that also informed method development. The benchmarks involve unseen molecular scaffolds and material composition groups. Across three acquisition budgets, CADA-OOD achieved higher mean out-of-distribution test scores than conventional acquisition strategies in most settings and stayed within 5% of the best method in all 21 benchmark and budget combinations. An approximation to Batch Active Learning by Diverse Gradient Embeddings (BADGE) showed comparable aggregate performance. Gains over conventional baselines were also observed with alternative molecular representations, with magnitudes varying across tasks. An external component comparison evaluated full CADA-OOD against a variant that removed only validation error relevance. Across three regression tasks under matched total label budgets, retaining this component yielded a mean relative reduction of 3.37% in root mean squared error (95% confidence interval 1.30−6.14%). Additional comparisons at equal total labeling cost, including a neural predictor with loss-based and gradient-based acquisition, showed task-dependent effects. These findings support validation error relevance as an interpretable complement to uncertainty and diversity for active acquisition under hidden distribution shift.

papers.title: WEVO: World Model-Enabled VLA Optimization for Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.

papers.title: Verify2Act: Critic-Guided Latent World Models for Verifying Language-Conditioned Manipulation Plans
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3\% task success, compared with 61.7\% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3\% for the VLM alone, and 46.7\% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30$\times$ fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.

papers.title: Ferrofluid Shape Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and manipulate objects. Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging. Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the fluid's dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium. Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning to control these transient shapes. Learning directly through physical interaction, our policies select current commands for a single fixed electromagnet based on visual observations, guiding the moving ferrofluid toward prescribed geometries. The learned policies repeatedly attain a variety of shapes spanning polygons, asterisks and pentominoes. These results demonstrate that learning directly from physical interaction enables reliable fluid shaping, opening new possibilities for controlling ferrofluid-based soft robots.

papers.title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

papers.title: Identity World Model: Recognizing People in an Imagined Latent World
papers.abstract: Whole-body human recognition has advanced rapidly with large vision models. However, existing methods remain fragile under real-world variations, as they tie identity to transient cues such as clothing, texture, pose, or viewpoint. We argue that a robust recognizer should not merely learn to ignore these cues, but imagine how a person would be represented if they changed. To this end, we propose IDWorld, an identity world model: just as a latent world model predicts the features of a scene after an action, IDWorld predicts how a person would be represented under a changed condition. In a single forward pass, IDWorld imagines these counterfactual features under shared canonical conditions, such as the same outfit, a fixed view, or a bare silhouette, without rendering any pixels. Compared with explicit imagination in pixels, this latent imagination keeps nearly the same accuracy while being over 11x faster, at 5.9 ms per frame. Since each imagined condition has its own strengths, IDWorld then fuses them adaptively, weighting each condition for every probe-gallery pair. Extensive experiments show that IDWorld achieves state-of-the-art results on CCPG and CCGR-MINI, outperforms the compared methods on MEVID, and generalizes best to CASIA-B* and SUSTech1K, with the best mAP on CCVID. These results suggest identity world models offer a simple yet effective path to robust recognition. Code will be released.

papers.title: From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger
papers.abstract: Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.

papers.title: MADJEPA: Enhanced Multi-Stage Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for Medical Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection in medical images is a complex task, requiring the development of a robust model using only healthy patient data. Without access to labeled data, modern approaches typically employ self-supervised learning to obtain a model of normality. Since world models promise to build strong internal representations of their environment, we consider them as suitable candidates for the medical anomaly detection environment, namely medical investigations of healthy patients. To this end, we propose MADJEPA, a medical anomaly detector based on an enhanced multi-stage joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). We design a multi-stage training pipeline to produce a robust detector: (1) image-based JEPA (I-JEPA) training aims to learn a strong representation of normal training data; (2) target encoder distillation aims to modulate over-generalization of I-JEPA representations to abnormal data; (3) pseudo-anomaly classification aims to calibrate anomaly predictions by learning a tight boundary around the normal data manifold. To demonstrate our design, we carry out comprehensive experiments on six datasets covering various medical image domains (e.g.~MRI, OCT, X-ray, histopathology), comparing our MADJEPA with numerous state-of-the-art methods. The results show that our carefully designed world model, MADJEPA, attains competitive results, ranking first on three datasets. Our ablation studies further confirm the utility of each training stage, indicating that I-JEPA alone is not sufficient to obtain competitive results in medical anomaly detection. We publicly release our code at https://github.com/Sabina085/madjepa.

papers.title: PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.

llm.why_not_core: It only accelerates PINN training via a meta-learned optimizer and reports no surrogate-based FEA speedup, no uncertainty quantification, no implant or biomechanics application, and no constraint handling.

papers.title: Old-School Planners Drive (Sometimes) Better Than Learned Ones
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models learn to plan from data, and hand-written planners are widely treated as a thing of the past. We test whether this is justified: we implement sixteen textbook planners, each combining a path source (reference line, A*, hybrid A*, RRT*) with a trajectory method (Frenet lattice, nonlinear optimization, $s$--$t$ search, dynamic window), and evaluate them on three benchmarks: open loop on nuScenes, closed loop on nuPlan with ground-truth perception, and photorealistic closed loop on HUGSIM. On HUGSIM, they replace only the planner of the end-to-end model UniAD and read its frozen perception, without an HD map or other privileged information. On nuScenes and nuPlan, the best textbook planners are competitive (L2 error of 0.735\,m against 0.947\,m for UniAD's planner; a nuPlan score of 79.3 against 76.1 for the rule-based PDM-Closed on Test14-hard with reactive agents). On HUGSIM, nine of the sixteen score above UniAD's learned planner on the same perception,. The best, a hybrid A* path followed by nonlinear trajectory optimization, raises HUGSIM's driving score (HD-Score) from 32.0 to 41.8. The gain is largest with standing and oncoming cars; against cars that steer at the ego, there is none. In 31 of the 182 runs in which UniAD's planner hits a car, the best textbook planner completes the route on the same perception: these crashes are due to the planner, not the perception.

papers.title: GEMS: Generation and Experience Memory for Subgoal-Guided Long-Horizon World Model Planning
papers.abstract: Visual world models enable effective short-horizon goal-conditioned planning, such as reaching nearby targets and pushing objects over short distances, by predicting candidate action outcomes and comparing their representations with a goal representation. However, extending this approach to long-horizon tasks is challenging: prediction errors accumulate over extended rollouts, while latent-space similarity to distant goals provides limited guidance for ranking candidate outcomes. Existing methods address these limitations by introducing intermediate subgoals, either generated by learned models or selected from experience memory. Generated subgoals can contain hallucinations or be inaccurate in aspects such as object positions and timing. Memory-based approaches are constrained by experience coverage and may lack precise guidance for selecting appropriate intermediate states from stored observations. We introduce GEMS, which generates temporally structured subgoals to guide action search and state selection from Latent Experience Memory (LEM). A distance gate determines whether predicted outcomes are evaluated against the generated subgoal or the selected memory state. Experiments across six tasks and task suites spanning manipulation, navigation, and reaching demonstrate the effectiveness of GEMS for long-horizon planning. GEMS outperforms state-of-the-art world-model planning baselines across different manipulation settings, achieving success rates of 92.8% on Cube, 68.4% on Push-T, and 54.1% on Meta-World. It improves over the strongest evaluated baseline on these tasks by 24.0, 7.3, and 22.2 percentage points, respectively. These results demonstrate that generated subgoals and experience memory can jointly strengthen long-horizon planning with a frozen world model.

papers.title: Temporal Extrapolation of Elastic Seismic Wave Propagation in Layered Media Using Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Temporal prediction of seismic velocity fields beyond the time interval represented in training remains challenging for neural operator models. This study develops a coupled neural operator framework for stress-conditioned temporal prediction in layered elastic media. A time-integrator-embedded Deep Operator Network (TI-DeepONet) advances the velocity field through an embedded fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) scheme, while a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learns a residual correction to the predicted spatial field. The two components are trained jointly in a predictor-corrector configuration. Prediction is initialized with reference velocity fields at the first two time levels and proceeds autoregressively, with reference stress fields and prescribed excitation supplied throughout rollout, including beyond the training interval. Four cases consider horizontally polarized shear (SH) waves in four-layer soil columns with fixed total depths of 50 and 280 m, excited by third-order Gaussian-derivative (DOG3) wavelets with central frequencies between 0.5 and 6 Hz. Layer thicknesses and shear-wave velocities vary across profiles. Evaluations on test profiles extend beyond the training interval by up to twice its duration. The predictions reproduce principal velocity arrivals and depth-dependent response patterns, with accuracy varying across profiles. Across the four cases, mean peak-normalized root-mean-square errors (NRMSEs) range from 0.53% to 2.31% over the full evaluation windows and from 0.61% to 2.82% over the extrapolation intervals. Both metrics use each profile's peak absolute reference velocity over the full evaluation window as the normalizer. These results demonstrate temporal velocity prediction under reference-stress conditioning for the tested configurations; autonomous continuation of the coupled velocity-stress wavefield remains to be established.

papers.title: HapBO: Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
papers.abstract: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($π: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $α$-$π$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

papers.title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
papers.abstract: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.

papers.title: Risk-optimal active learning with informative abstention
papers.abstract: We study label acquisition when an oracle may abstain and its response probability shares parameters with the classifier. A query can then provide information through both a returned label and the response outcome. Under a correctly specified parametric model, we derive the classifier information after adjustment for response-model nuisance parameters. Combining this information with the local curvature of multiclass zero-one risk gives an acquisition criterion for minimizing the leading asymptotic excess risk. We characterize the optimal allocation under a fixed query budget and show how query allocation affects response identifiability. The oracle criterion reduces to response-discounted acquisition when response probability does not depend on the classifier parameters. Simulations examine the resulting query allocations and isolate the contribution of the response-outcome term through an ablation. A Consumer Complaints replay retains observed human abstentions and reveals benchmark labels upon response. Response-aware acquisition has lower mean test error than response-discounted acquisition at the two largest budgets, with paired differences significant after Holm correction. Entropy sampling performs better at the smallest budget. The gains depend on the response mechanism and query budget.

papers.title: Profile-Driven Deep Learning for Rapid Evaluation of Piston Skirt Contact Pressure
papers.abstract: To address the issue of excessive computational time consumption associated with finite element analysis in calculating the contact pressure distribution of the internal combustion engine piston skirt, this study proposes a deep learning–based mapping approach from low-dimensional geometric parameters to high-dimensional images. The improved U-Net model embedded with a convolutional block attention module, bilinear upsampling, and partitioned weighted hybrid loss function is augmented with an extra feature projection layer to boost mapping performance. The results indicate that the proposed model shows good agreement with the numerical simulation results in forecasting the contact pressure distribution. The mean absolute percentage error of the prediction results is below 7%, and each independent prediction requires approximately 2.8 s, demonstrating the computational efficiency of the proposed surrogate model. Under the maximum-torque condition, the proposed method reproduced the overall thrust side contact pressure distribution of unseen profiles, demonstrating its capability as a rapid surrogate model for piston skirt contact pressure evaluation within the parameter range.

papers.title: Revealing the osseointegration potential of Mg-based implants: A multilevel comparison of ZX00, PLGA and titanium screws in an ovine preclinical model
papers.abstract: Absorbable materials like polymers and magnesium (Mg) exhibit promising characteristics as orthopedic implants. Mg-based implants offer bone-like mechanical properties with an adequate osteogenic potential and a stable degradation pattern. Here we investigated the osseointegration, biocompatibility, degradation, performance and biomechanical properties of a Mg-based alloy (ZX00) over 26 weeks (w) in comparison to absorbable poly-L-lactic-co-glycolide acid (PLGA) and state-of-the-art titanium (Ti), implanted into an ovine model. ZX00, PLGA, and Ti screws were bicortically implanted into the tibiae of 33 sheep. To assess implant behavior, we performed in vivo X-ray imaging and computed tomography (CT) and ex vivo high-resolution µCT. Furthermore, systemic and local biocompatibility was investigated by histology. Novel push-out biomechanical testing complemented the osseointegration assessment. We observed close bone-to-implant contact across all groups and progressive degradation of ZX00 implants accompanied by increased cortical bone apposition, also observed in the PLGA and Ti groups. Osseointegration and biocompatibility of ZX00 implants were observed with no signs of systemic toxicity comparable to PLGA or Ti. Biomechanical testing demonstrated consistency in force required to push out ZX00 screws. ZX00 was comparable to PLGA and Ti implants regarding osseointegration, mechanical stability and biocompatibility. This study demonstrates that ZX00 combines progressive degradation with sustained osseointegration and functional fixation stability, making it an appropriate absorbable alternative in orthopedic surgery and providing new insight into the relationship between degradation, biological response and implant stability.

papers.title: Revisiting the gold standard: why 2-stage revision THA remains relevant for hip PJI: a 10-year experience with excellent infection-free survival
papers.abstract: Background: 2-stage revision total hip arthroplasty (THA) remains the reference standard for the management of hip periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), despite increasing interest in 1-stage revision. This study reports the 10-year experience of a tertiary referral centre and evaluates infection control, implant survivorship, functional outcomes, and complications following staged revision. Methods: A retrospective review of prospectively collected data was performed for patients undergoing staged revision THA for hip PJI between 2014 and 2024. 65 patients met the inclusion criteria and were followed for a mean of 69.3 ± 28.9 months. Functional outcomes were assessed using the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS). Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to determine implant survivorship, with reoperation, re-revision, recurrent infection, or mortality within 1 year of PJI treatment as survival endpoints. Results: An infection-free survival of 97.0% (63/65) was achieved at final follow-up. Only 2 patients (3.1%) developed recurrent infection, managed with debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) ( n = 1) or repeat 2-stage revision ( n = 1). Overall, implant survivorship was 87.6% (57/65). The remaining reoperations were attributable to mechanical failures, including aseptic loosening ( n = 3, 4.6%), recurrent dislocation ( n = 1, 1.5%), and periprosthetic fracture ( n = 1, 1.5%). The mean mHHS improved significantly from 26.0 ± 11.8 preoperatively to 68.9 ± 7.4 at final follow-up (mean improvement, 42.9 ± 9.6; p < 0.001). Conclusions: 2-stage revision THA provides excellent infection control, high implant survivorship, and significant functional improvement in patients with hip PJI. These findings reinforce its continued role as a reliable and reproducible treatment strategy, particularly in complex patients managed in real-world clinical practice.

papers.title: Apparent liner–head incongruity on immediate postoperative radiographs after total hip arthroplasty
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Apparent liner-head incongruity is occasionally observed on immediate postoperative radiographs after total hip arthroplasty (THA), but its clinical significance remains unclear. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 155 patients (190 hips) who underwent primary THA using a robotic-arm-assisted system. 3 orthopaedic surgeons independently assessed immediate postoperative radiographs for apparent liner-head incongruity. Serial radiographs were reviewed to evaluate the subsequent clinical course. RESULTS: Apparent liner-head incongruity was identified in 12 of 190 hips (6.3%; 95% confidence interval [CI], 3.3-10.8%). In the sensitivity analysis restricted to 1 hip per patient, apparent liner-head incongruity was identified in 9 of 155 hips (5.8%; 95% CI, 2.7-10.7%). All 12 hips subsequently demonstrated restoration of normal radiographic congruity without surgical intervention. No radiographic abnormalities or clinical complications were identified during follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Apparent liner-head incongruity on immediate postoperative radiographs may be transient and does not invariably indicate persistent mechanical incongruity. Recognition of this phenomenon may aid interpretation of unexpected postoperative radiographic findings, although true mechanical abnormalities should be carefully excluded.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Printable Human Platelet Lysate Methacrylate/Hyaluronic Acid Methacrylate/Nanohydroxyapatite Nanocomposite Hydrogels with Enhanced Mechanical and Rheological Properties for Tissue Engineering
papers.abstract: Human platelet lysate-based hydrogels have gained increasing attention as a xeno-free platform for tissue engineering due to their potential to support cell viability and biological activity. Human-derived platelet lysate methacrylate (hPLMA) is a recently developed photocrosslinkable material that enables the formation of three-dimensional (3D) hydrogels through light-induced crosslinking of blood-derived proteins. However, evaluating hPLMA in different hydrogel formulations may provide further insight into its potential for advanced applications. In this study, hyaluronic acid methacrylate (HAMA, 1% w/v) and nanohydroxyapatite (nHAp, 5% w/v) were incorporated into hPLMA to develop a photocrosslinkable nanocomposite hydrogel (hPLMA/HAMA/nHAp). The incorporation of HAMA increased the compressive strength from 2.1 ± 0.9 kPa to 4.5 ± 1.5 kPa, resulting in an approximately 40-fold increase in the storage modulus while preserving shear-thinning behavior. The composite hydrogels exhibited sustained release of platelet-derived growth factor-AB (PDGF-AB) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) over 9 days and supported human adipose stem cell (hASC) viability (>93% for all formulations). Furthermore, extrusion-based 3D printing enabled the fabrication of grid-shaped constructs with maintained porosity, demonstrating moderate printability and shape fidelity of the constructs. While the independent contribution of nHAp remains to be investigated in future studies, the results demonstrate that the incorporation of HAMA improves the mechanical and rheological properties of the hPLMA/nHAp hydrogel, highlighting its potential for future tissue engineering applications.

papers.title: Multi-performance optimization of CO2-MQL burnishing process considering surface properties
papers.abstract: In this work, process parameters of the CO 2 -based minimum quantity lubrication burnishing (CMB) process, including the spindle speed ( S ), feed rate ( f ), and penetration depth ( D ) are optimized to maximize the Vickers hardness ( VH ) and reduce the maximum height roughness in the defined area ( Sz ). A set of CMB experiments was conducted on SKD61 steel. The Gaussian process regression (GPR) and ensembles of trees (ET) approaches were used to propose predictive models of the CMB responses. The criteria importance through intercriteria correlation (CRITIC), elite-guided adaptive Cauchy-zebra optimization algorithm (ECZOA), and multi-attributive ideal-real comparative analysis (MAIRCA) are utilized to compute the weights, generate feasible solutions, and determine the best point. The findings showed that the optimal S , f , and D were 1600 rpm, 100 mm/min, and 0.20 mm, respectively. At the optimal point, the improvements in the VH and Sz were 5.5% and 30.0%, respectively. Moreover, the average coefficient of friction ( COF ) and final wear depth ( Z ) were reduced from approximately 0.704 to 0.581 and from 0.17 to 0.08 mm, respectively, demonstrating the improved tribological performance of the optimized CMB process. The GPR approach outperformed the ET model in predicting the CMB responses. The integrated GPR-ECZOA-MAIRCA procedure successfully identified a beneficial operating condition for simultaneously improving Sz and VH within the investigated parameter domain. Microstructural observations revealed that higher S and D promoted more extensive subsurface deformation. The compressive residual stress (CRS) of − 412.48 MPa was obtained, demonstrating the development of substantial compressive stresses and improved surface integrity in the burnished SKD61 steel.

papers.title: Ontology-grounded nanotoxicity data federation with a provenance-aware knowledge graph and conformal prediction for antimicrobial hazard screening
papers.abstract: Nanomaterials are increasingly used across industrial, therapeutic, and consumer applications, while their interactions with biological and environmental systems can produce adverse effects. Although nanotoxicological evidence is abundant, it remains fragmented across curated repositories, computational archives, and datasets extracted from the scientific literature. Inconsistent terminology, measurement units, and identifier schemes limit interoperability and reuse. This study presents an ontology-grounded pipeline that federates two complementary public sources against the eNanoMapper ontology, harmonises records into a canonical schema, preserves evidence in a provenance-aware knowledge graph, and applies gradient-boosted classification with split conformal prediction to a relative antimicrobial hazard-screening task based on MIC/MBC records. The integrated dataset contains 6588 records spanning thirteen material classes and seven harmonised endpoint types, and the knowledge graph contains 2279 nodes and 32,940 typed edges in one weakly connected component. Under five-fold stratified cross-validation, the strongest classifier achieved an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC) of \(0.819 \pm 0.020\) . On a disjoint test set, split conformal prediction achieved empirical marginal coverage of 0.955, 0.929, and 0.825 against nominal targets of 0.95, 0.90, and 0.80, respectively. A material-grouped cross-validation stress test reduced AUROC to \(0.609 \pm 0.098\) , demonstrating limited generalisation to unseen material classes. Feature attribution and ablation show that categorical experimental context carries most of the discriminative signal, whereas measured physicochemical descriptors contribute comparatively little. The resulting framework therefore combines semantic data integration, explicit provenance, and uncertainty-aware antimicrobial hazard screening while making the limits of cross-material generalisation explicit.

papers.title: Physics‐informed surrogate modelling for intermittent wheat drying: Fractional kinetics, Arrhenius generalization, and cross‐condition prediction
papers.abstract: Intermittent grain drying induces non‐Markovian, sub‐diffusive moisture transport that classical Fickian and curve‐by‐curve empirical models cannot intrinsically generalize. This work establishes a unified k ( T , I ) structural requirement, k ( T , I ) = k 0 exp.(− E ₐ/RT)· I ᵝ, that simultaneously governs empirical thin‐layer models, the fractional Mittag‐Leffler parametric model, and a fractional physics‐informed machine learning (fPIML) framework. Experiments on BRS‐Jacana wheat at three temperatures (40, 55, and 70°C) and two intermittency periods (5 and 10 min) yielded 152 gravimetric observations on eight drying curves. Two‐stage globalization of six empirical benchmarks confirmed Arrhenius activation energies of 22–42 kJ mol −1 ( R 2 ≥ 0.91) for the physically well‐behaved models (Page, Logarithmic, Midilli), while the fractional‐parametric model yielded E ₐ = 33.9 kJ mol −1 and a global law α ( T , I ) ≈ −1.28 + 803.4/Tᵅ − 0.246·ln(I) ( R 2 = 0.844). The fPIML embeds the Caputo fractional governing equation Dₜᵅ(MR) + λ ᵅ( T , I )·MR = 0 into the training loss, with λ ᵅ structured as a learned Arrhenius expression. Under thermal leave‐one‐temperature‐out validation, the fPIML (RMSE = 0.0479, R 2 = 0.955) achieves lower RMSE and higher explained variance than both the integer‐order PINN (RMSE = 0.0604, R 2 = 0.929) and the data‐only ANN (RMSE = 0.0795, R 2 = 0.875). Under the critical intermittency extrapolation test, trained exclusively on I = 5 min and tested on I = 10 min, the fPIML achieves the lowest MAE (0.059) among all models; the integer‐order PINN reaches R 2 = 0.504 but with an MAE 90% higher (0.112), while the data‐only ANN collapses to R 2 = −0.025.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of imaging techniques for aseptic loosening in total hip arthroplasty; a systematic review
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: As the number of total hip arthroplasties (THAs) performed worldwide increases, the burden of revision surgery rises, with aseptic loosening being a leading cause. Diagnostic imaging strategies remain suboptimal, potentially leading to unnecessary revision or undertreatment. This systematic review aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of imaging modalities for detecting aseptic loosening in THA, using intraoperative findings as the reference standard. METHODS: This PRISMA-compliant systematic review included a search in PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Eligible studies included adult patients with suspected aseptic loosening of THA, comparing at least one imaging modality to the intraoperative finding. Risk of bias was assessed using the QUADAS-2 tool. Diagnostic performance metrics were extracted or calculated. RESULTS: The search and selection yielded 11 articles. Imaging modalities included plain radiography, CT-scans, SPECT/CT, FDG-PET, bone scintigraphy, arthrography, and MRI. Risk of bias was high in all studies, primarily related to patient selection and applicability of the reference standard. The overall certainty of evidence ranged from low to moderate. Dual-energy CT and inducible motion CT showed the highest reported diagnostic performance, based on single-centre studies. CONCLUSIONS: All included studies demonstrated a high risk of bias, and surgeons were not blinded at the time of revision surgery. As a result, no reliable diagnostic strategy can currently be recommended. The favorable findings for CT-based techniques are hypothesis-generating. Methodologically robust, double-blinded studies are required to determine the true accuracy of advanced imaging techniques.PROSPERO registration number:CRD42024584480.

papers.title: Use of morselized bone allograft in revision hip arthroplasty for massive acetabular defect: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Introduction: Several surgical options are available for the revision of large acetabular defects, but the optimal reconstruction technique remains controversial. This meta-analysis evaluated the failure rates of Paprosky type III or American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) type III–IV acetabular defects treated with morselized allograft combined with a cemented cup, cementless cup, or reinforcement device. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews was performed for studies published between January 1980 and April 2024. Eligible studies included revision total hip arthroplasty (THA) using acetabular impaction bone grafting for large acetabular defects. The primary outcome was implant failure at a mean follow-up of approximately 9 years. Results: Thirty-nine studies were included, comprising 41 treatment cohorts: morselized allograft with a cemented cup (10 studies), cementless cup (9 studies), or reinforcement device (22 studies). The overall implant failure rate was 2.1% (95% CI, 1.6–2.8%) at a mean follow-up of 9.2 years. Failure rates did not differ significantly among treatment groups: 1.6% (95% CI, 0.9–2.6%) for cemented cups, 2.1% (95% CI, 1.4–3.2%) for cementless cups, and 2.5% (95% CI, 1.7–3.7%) for reinforcement devices (p = 0.351). Aseptic loosening was the leading cause of failure (80.5%), followed by infection (13.1%) and dislocation (6.4%). Compared with cemented cups, reinforcement devices were associated with higher rates of infection (3.6% vs. 0.7%, p = 0.001) and dislocation (1.4% vs. 0.6%, p = 0.010). Conclusions: Morselized allograft provides low failure rates in the revision of large acetabular defects regardless of the implant used. However, reinforcement devices are associated with a higher risk of re-revision due to infection and dislocation.

papers.title: FAILURE OF INTERNAL FIXATION IN DISPLACED FEMORAL NECK FRACTURES: CLINICAL AND RADIOGRAPHIC CHARACTERISTICS AND OUTCOME AFTER A CONVERSION TO TOTAL HIP ARTHROPLASTY
papers.abstract: Introduction: Internal fixation of displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures may fail through nonunion, avascular necrosis, or mechanical complications. This study describes the clinical and radiographic characteristics of patients with failed fixation and reports quality-of-life outcomes after conversion to total hip arthroplasty. Material and Methods: We retrospectively reviewed 28 patients (18 men, 10 women; age 40–65 years) treated between June 2018 and June 2023 at a single university trauma centre. All had initially undergone closed reduction and internal fixation for a displaced (Garden III–IV) femoral neck fracture and subsequently required revision for fixation-related complications. Radiographic bone quality, reduction quality, and cannulated-screw position were reviewed. All patients underwent hardware removal and conversion to total hip arthroplasty. Quality of life was assessed using the SF-36 before revision and during 12 months of follow-up. Results: Eleven patients (39.3%) presented with avascular necrosis and 17 (60.7%) with nonunion or mechanical fixation failure. The Singh index at presentation was 4–6. All patients underwent conversion to total hip arthroplasty (21 uncemented and 7 cemented). In the avascular-necrosis subgroup, mean physical component summary score increased from 40.27 before revision to 52.27 at 12 months and mean mental component summary score from 40.45 to 54.72. In the nonunion/fixation-failure subgroup, the corresponding scores increased from 41.11 to 53.23 and from 42.05 to 54.00. Conclusion: Failed internal fixation in this series frequently occurred despite relatively preserved radiographic bone quality and was commonly accompanied by suboptimal reduction and/or screw configuration. Conversion to total hip arthroplasty was associated with substantial improvement in patient-reported quality of life during the first postoperative year. Keywords: femoral neck fracture; nonunion; avascular necrosis; internal fixation failure; conversion total hip arthroplasty; SF-36.

papers.title: Improving the wear resistance of additively manufactured aluminum alloy components by plasma electrolytic polishing and microarc oxidation
papers.abstract: This study evaluated a two-stage post-treatment for AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy components made by selective laser melting. The treatment consisted of plasma electrolytic polishing (PEP) followed by microarc oxidation (MAO). Polishing made the surface profile more uniform, and subsequent MAO produced a more uniform ceramic-like coating than MAO on an unpolished surface. The effectiveness of the two-stage treatment was assessed in abrasive wear tests and in dry-sliding tests using a shaft–bushing configuration. After the abrasion tests, specimens coated by MAO without prior polishing exhibited severe damage, including adhesive seizure, microcutting, and deep localized craters. Prepolished specimens had a smoother, more uniform worn surface with no signs of galling. In the dry-sliding tests, the two-stage treatment gave the largest reductions in the coefficient of friction (39 %) and mass loss (80 %) relative to untreated specimens. The dominant wear mechanism changed from microcutting to low-cycle frictional fatigue of the surface layers undergoing plastic deformation.

papers.title: Physics-informed neural networks for subject-specific recovery of travelling-wave structure in resting-state fMRI
papers.abstract: Resting-state BOLD fluctuations show reproducible spatiotemporal propagation that is not accounted for by conventional zero-lag functional connectivity. Travelling wave analyses based on phase gradients or statistical decomposition have problems when multiple wave generators overlap or when wave origins must be localized. This work introduces a wave-informed physics-informed neural network that represents the parcellated BOLD signal as a superposition of seven spatially extended damped travelling wave generators, each periodically re-excited at its own characteristic frequency and fixed at initialization to one of the seven canonical Schaefer resting-state networks. A soft anatomical prior derived from each subject’s diffusion-tensor structural connectivity is included to encode the hypothesis that white-matter pathways constrain wave direction. The pipeline is validated on synthetic data by three simulation studies, creating the operating envelope, and then applied to 41 cognitively normal participants of the ADNI-3 cohort. A within-subject ablation showed that mean alignment between recovered wave directions and underlying white-matter geometry increased by a small but statistically detectable amount when using the structural prior (one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p = 0.026), with exploratory network-level effects most evident in the visual, dorsal-attention, and salience/ventral-attention networks. The contribution is a network-anchored parametric inverse method returning subject-specific propagation descriptors from short resting-state scans.

papers.title: Strengthening Primary School Teachers' Teaching Competencies Through Deep Learning Training At SDN 007 Bengkong
papers.abstract: This study aims to analyze the effectiveness of deep learning training in strengthening the teaching competence of elementary school teachers at SDN 007 Bengkong. This research used a quantitative approach with a one group pretest posttest design. The subjects of the study were teachers at SDN 007 Bengkong who participated in deep learning training. Data were collected using a teaching competence test before and after the training. The data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, the N-Gain test, and the paired sample t-test. The results showed that the average pretest score of 68.44 increased to 84.17 in the posttest. The N-Gain score was 0.51, which falls into the moderate category. The paired sample t-test showed a significance value of 0.000, indicating a significant difference in teachers’ teaching competence before and after the training. These findings indicate that deep learning training is effective in improving teachers’ competence, especially in learning reflection, formative assessment, lesson planning, learning implementation, and active learning strategies. This study recommends that schools continue teacher training through mentoring, teacher learning communities, and academic supervision to ensure sustainable improvement in teaching competence.

papers.title: Integration Of Small Games In Physical Education Learning: A Literature Review On Character Formation And Student Self-Efficacy
papers.abstract: Physical Education often emphasizes technical drills and motor achievement, so character formation and students' self-efficacy are not always designed as explicit learning outcomes. This article aims to analyze the integration of small games in Physical Education learning for character formation and the improvement of students' self-efficacy. This study used a narrative literature review with a thematic approach. Nine main articles were analyzed based on author, title, index, main findings, and relevance to the research focus. The findings show that small games, traditional games, small-sided games, student-centered learning, self-regulated learning, and game-based physical activities contribute to active engagement, motivation, cooperation, responsibility, discipline, sportsmanship, and self-efficacy. The review also indicates that character formation does not occur automatically through play. Teachers need to design explicit character objectives, modify games, provide feedback, and facilitate reflection. This study concludes that small games can serve as a relevant pedagogical strategy in Physical Education when they are designed systematically, inclusively, and based on active learning principles.
